findings.title: Revision validation rejects valid git revisions containing spaces
findings.description: _revision now rejects any value containing whitespace. Git accepts revision syntax with spaces, such as date-based reflog selectors like HEAD@{2 weeks ago}. Before this change those values were passed to git and worked. Now they raise ValueError, and the CLI exits with status 2 and a 'not a git revision' message. The check also rejects an empty until value, which previously meant since..HEAD.
findings.suggestion: Only reject values starting with '-' (the option-injection risk), and rely on the '--' separator and git's own error reporting for everything else. If empty values must be rejected, check only for emptiness.

findings.title: Expired sessions are no longer evicted on access, so they accumulate until purge_expired runs
findings.description: The previous get() deleted a session once it was found expired. The new get() just returns None and leaves the entry in the map. Nothing in this change calls purge_expired, so in a long-running process that never calls it, every expired session stays in memory (and in the persisted JSON file for FileSessionStore) indefinitely. Memory and file size grow with total logins over the process lifetime, not with live sessions.
findings.suggestion: Either call purge_expired periodically from the application, or have get() evict the expired entry under the write lock as before, so that the eviction behaviour is preserved.

findings.title: Every create copies the whole session map, and FileSessionStore rewrites and fsyncs the full file under the lock
findings.description: create() builds a new dict from all existing sessions on every login, which is O(n) per call. For FileSessionStore, _commit also serialises every session, writes a temp file and calls fsync while holding _write_lock. Under concurrent logins, all requests queue behind one full-file fsync, so latency grows with the number of live sessions and login throughput drops sharply.
findings.suggestion: Mutate a private dict under the lock for the in-memory store, and for the file store batch or debounce persistence, or append individual changes instead of rewriting the whole file on each login.

findings.title: get() no longer evicts expired sessions, so expired entries accumulate
findings.description: The previous get() deleted a session once it was found expired. The new version only returns None, so an expired session stays in the dict until purge_expired() is called. Nothing in this change schedules purge_expired(), so a process that issues many logins and never purges will hold every expired session in memory, and FileSessionStore will keep persisting them to disk.
findings.suggestion: Restore lazy eviction: when the session is expired, drop it under the write lock (for example by calling revoke with the raw token or by a digest-based removal), or document and enforce a periodic purge_expired() call.

findings.title: Bare except and unguarded unlink can mask the original write error
findings.description: The bare except catches BaseException, and os.unlink(tmp_name) runs without a guard. If the failure happened after os.replace moved the file, or if the temp file is already gone, unlink raises FileNotFoundError and replaces the real exception. If fdopen fails before the fd is wrapped, the descriptor is also left open.
findings.suggestion: Use `except BaseException:` at minimum, wrap the unlink in `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)`, and close fd if os.fdopen raises before it takes ownership.

findings.title: Every create() copies the whole session map and rewrites the entire file
findings.description: create() builds a new dict from all sessions, and FileSessionStore._commit then serialises all of them and fsyncs the file. Each login therefore costs O(n) memory and O(n) disk I/O with an fsync, so login latency and write amplification grow with the number of live sessions.
findings.suggestion: Persist incremental changes (for example an append-only log with periodic compaction) or batch writes, instead of rewriting the full snapshot on every create.

findings.title: create() copies the whole session map on every login
findings.description: Each create() builds a new dict from all existing sessions via {**self._sessions, ...} and then replaces the store, so each login costs O(n) in the number of live sessions. For FileSessionStore, _commit also re-serialises and rewrites the whole file with fsync. Under load with many active sessions, login latency and write amplification grow with the total session count.
findings.suggestion: Mutate a private dict under the write lock and publish a copy only when readers need a snapshot, or keep a single dict and do the file write with the lock held. Consider batching or deferring persistence if per-login fsync is too costly.

findings.title: Expired sessions are no longer evicted on lookup
findings.description: The previous get() deleted an expired session it found. The new get() only returns None, so expired entries stay in the map until purge_expired() is called. If nothing calls purge_expired on a schedule, memory and the persisted file grow without bound with every expired login.
findings.suggestion: Either evict the expired entry in get() under the write lock, as before, or confirm that a periodic purge_expired() call is wired up and document that requirement.

findings.title: File descriptor leaks if os.fdopen fails
findings.description: If os.fdopen(fd, ...) raises, the raw descriptor from mkstemp is never closed, and the temp file is then unlinked by the bare except without the fd being released. Repeated failures can exhaust descriptors.
findings.suggestion: Wrap fdopen in the try block, or close fd explicitly if fdopen raises. Also replace the bare except with except BaseException so the intent is clear.

findings.title: remove() no longer reports a failed delete
findings.description: The original remove() raised UnknownProduct when repository.delete(sku) returned False. The new code ignores the return value. If the row disappears between _fetch and delete (for example, a concurrent remove in another process), remove() reports success and _forget still runs, so callers no longer get the not-found signal they relied on.
findings.suggestion: Restore the check: if not self._repository.delete(sku): raise UnknownProduct(sku), and only call _forget after a successful delete.

findings.title: remove() ignores the repository's delete result, so a concurrent delete now succeeds silently
findings.description: The old code raised UnknownProduct when repository.delete returned False. The new code fetches first and then ignores the return value. If another request deletes the same SKU between the fetch and the delete, this call returns normally instead of raising UnknownProduct, which changes the behaviour callers relied on.
findings.suggestion: Keep the contract by checking the return value: if not self._repository.delete(sku): raise UnknownProduct(sku), and only call _forget after a successful delete.

findings.title: Any invalidation anywhere discards every in-flight load, so the cache stops storing under write churn
findings.description: The generation counter is global, so any invalidate() or invalidate_where() call, including one for an unrelated SKU, prevents get_or_load from storing its loaded value. Under steady write traffic most loads are never cached, so every storefront read goes to the repository and the cache gives little benefit.
findings.suggestion: Track generations per key, or accept the staleness trade-off and document it. Per-key generations would let unrelated writes keep caching.

findings.title: remove() ignores the repository's delete result, so a concurrent removal is reported as success
findings.description: The old code raised UnknownProduct when repository.delete(sku) returned False. The new code calls _fetch first and then ignores the return value of delete. If another request deletes the same SKU between the fetch and the delete, this call returns normally and still invalidates the cache, instead of raising UnknownProduct as before. Callers that rely on the exception to detect a lost race will treat a failed removal as successful.
findings.suggestion: Restore the check: if not self._repository.delete(sku): raise UnknownProduct(sku), and only call _forget after a successful delete.

findings.title: Rename is not made durable by fsyncing the parent directory
findings.description: _atomic_write fsyncs the temp file before os.replace but never fsyncs the containing directory afterwards. After put()/put_stream()/copy() returns, a power loss or crash can leave the directory entry pointing at the previous blob, so a write the caller saw succeed is silently lost. Readers still never see a partial file, so this is a durability gap rather than corruption.
findings.suggestion: After os.replace(temp_path, target), open the parent directory with os.open(target.parent, os.O_RDONLY) and os.fsync it, closing the descriptor afterwards (skip or guard on platforms where this is unsupported).

findings.title: server_name.partition(":") breaks IPv6 literal server names
findings.description: The old urlsplit-based code parsed bracketed IPv6 hosts correctly, so SERVER_NAME="[::1]:5000" gave hostname "::1" and port 5000. partition(":") splits at the first colon, so sn_host becomes "[" and sn_port becomes ":1]:5000". When host is not given, run() then binds to "[", and int(sn_port) raises ValueError on ":1]:5000". The server fails to start for that configuration.
findings.suggestion: Keep urlsplit-style parsing, for example urlsplit(f"//{server_name}") and use .hostname and .port, or use rpartition/bracket-aware parsing that handles a leading '[' .

findings.title: Host split on first colon breaks IPv6 cookie domain
findings.description: The previous urlsplit(host_url).hostname handled bracketed IPv6 hosts. ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0] returns "[" for a host like "[::1]:80". Cookies set by responses from such a host are stored under the wrong domain, so they are not sent on later requests from the test client.
findings.suggestion: Restore hostname extraction that understands brackets, for example urlsplit(f"//{ctx.request.host}").hostname or "localhost", or strip the port with a bracket-aware helper.

findings.title: partition on ':' breaks IPv6 server_name values
findings.description: The old urlsplit(f"//{server_name}") parsing handled bracketed IPv6 literals such as "[::1]:5000", giving hostname "::1" and port 5000. server_name.partition(":") splits at the first colon, so sn_host becomes "[" and sn_port becomes ":1]:5000". The int(sn_port) call in the following branch then raises ValueError when run() is called with an IPv6 SERVER_NAME and no explicit port. The same change also drops hostname lowercasing and bracket stripping.
findings.suggestion: Keep urlsplit-based parsing, or handle a leading '[' by splitting on ']' first, and lowercase the host the same way urlsplit().hostname does.

findings.title: Cookie domain for IPv6 hosts is truncated to '['
findings.description: Replacing urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname with ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0] changes the domain passed to _update_cookies_from_response. For a request host like "[::1]:8000", the domain becomes "[" instead of "::1". Cookies set by the response are then stored under the wrong domain and are not sent back on later requests to that host. The hostname attribute also lowercased the value, which partition does not.
findings.suggestion: Use urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or "localhost" as before, or strip brackets and lowercase the host explicitly.

findings.title: IPv6 host is split at the first colon, so cookies are stored under the wrong domain
findings.description: ctx.request.host includes the port and, for IPv6 literals, brackets. Splitting on the first colon turns "[::1]:5000" into "[", and "[::1]" into "[". The previous urlsplit(...).hostname handled this correctly and returned "::1". With an IPv6 host, cookies set by the response are saved under the bogus domain "[" and are not sent back on later requests, so session and login state silently break in tests. The removed code also lowercased the hostname and fell back to "localhost" when it was empty, and the new code does neither.
findings.suggestion: Restore hostname parsing that handles brackets, for example urlsplit(f"//{ctx.request.host}").hostname or "localhost", or use werkzeug's own host splitting helper.

findings.title: SERVER_NAME parsing with partition() breaks bracketed IPv6 literals
findings.description: urlsplit(f"//{server_name}") handled "[::1]:5000" by returning hostname "::1" and port 5000. partition(":") returns sn_host "[" and sn_port ":1"-style garbage, so run() can receive host "[" and int() raises ValueError when the port is parsed. Previously this worked. This only triggers when SERVER_NAME is an IPv6 literal with a port.
findings.suggestion: Keep urlsplit-based parsing, or handle a leading '[' by splitting on ']' before taking the port.

findings.title: RootModel.__copy__ no longer carries over private attributes
findings.description: The removed block was the only place in this override that handled `__pydantic_private__`. The copy now never sets `m.__pydantic_private__`, so a shallow copy of a RootModel subclass that declares PrivateAttr fields gets no private state. Accessing those attributes on the copy will fail or return missing values. The removed code wrote to a `__dict__` key rather than the `__pydantic_private__` slot, so it was already not doing the right thing, but the copy still needs the private state transferred.
findings.suggestion: Copy the private storage into the slot explicitly, for example `private = self.__pydantic_private__; _object_setattr(m, '__pydantic_private__', None if private is None else {k: v for k, v in private.items() if v is not PydanticUndefined})`, and add a test that copies a RootModel with a private attribute.

findings.title: Reading a bytes UploadFile leaves its position at EOF, so later readers get empty bytes
findings.description: The removed helper saved the file position, read the content, and seeked back. The new code calls value.read() directly, so the UploadFile is left at end-of-file. _extract_form_body runs per dependant with the same FormData, so the same UploadFile object can reach more than one bytes-annotated parameter, for example two sub-dependencies that both declare the same form field as bytes. The first consumer gets the full content, but the second reads from EOF and receives b"". The same applies to any code that reads the UploadFile after this point.
findings.suggestion: Restore the original behaviour: record file.file.tell() before reading, read the content, and seek back in a finally block, or otherwise keep _read_file_bytes-style position restoration at both call sites.

findings.title: Bytes read from UploadFile no longer restores the file position
findings.description: The removed _read_file_bytes helper saved the file position, read the content, and seeked back. The new code calls value.read() directly, so the file cursor ends at EOF. Any later read of the same UploadFile now returns b'' instead of the content. This happens when a bytes-annotated field is processed and the same UploadFile object is read again afterwards, for example by another field that refers to it, by a later dependency, or by the endpoint itself. The same applies to the sequence branch at line 1078. Those callers would silently receive empty data.
findings.suggestion: Keep the position-preserving behaviour: record file.file.tell() before the read and seek back to it in a finally block, or restore the helper and call it from both sites.

findings.title: Removed position restore leaves the UploadFile at EOF after reading
findings.description: The removed _read_file_bytes helper restored the file position after reading. Now value.read() leaves the shared UploadFile at EOF. If the same UploadFile object is bound to another field in the same request (for example two parameters sharing one form alias, one typed bytes and one UploadFile), the second read returns b'' silently. This is an edge case, so the impact is limited.
findings.suggestion: Keep position restore around the read, or confirm each form key maps to one consumer and document that a file is consumed by its first read.

findings.title: Removing Sentinel.__reduce_ex__ breaks pickling and identity of UNSET/FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE
findings.description: The deleted __reduce_ex__ made pickling reconstruct the sentinel member by name via getattr(Sentinel, name), preserving singleton identity. Without it, Enum's default reduce uses the member's _value_ (a bare object()). Unpickling then calls Sentinel(<new object>), which raises ValueError, or yields a member that fails identity checks such as `value is UNSET`. Any Parameter or Option holding UNSET that is pickled, for example to send it to a worker process, will fail or lose its sentinel identity.
findings.suggestion: Restore __reduce_ex__ returning getattr, (self.__class__, self.name), or keep the removal only if pickling of these objects is confirmed unsupported and no caller relies on it.

findings.title: Removing __reduce_ex__ breaks pickling of the UNSET sentinels
findings.description: The deleted __reduce_ex__ made pickle serialise each sentinel by name via getattr(Sentinel, name). Without it, the default Enum reduction applies and pickles the member by its value, which is a bare object() instance. Unpickling then calls Sentinel(<new object>), which matches no member and raises ValueError. Any pickled Context, Parameter or default that holds UNSET or FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE, for example one sent to a multiprocessing worker, will fail to load. Copy and deepcopy are unaffected because Enum already returns self for them.
findings.suggestion: Restore __reduce_ex__ returning getattr, (self.__class__, self.name), or keep the method and only drop __copy__/__deepcopy__ if those are redundant.

findings.title: Removing Sentinel copy/pickle hooks breaks identity of UNSET and FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE
findings.description: The diff deletes the __copy__, __deepcopy__ and __reduce_ex__ overrides that made copy and pickle return the same singleton member. Without them, copy.copy or copy.deepcopy may not return the same member, and pickling falls back to Enum's default reduce, which serialises the underlying object() value. On unpickling, Sentinel(<new object>) cannot find the original value and raises ValueError, or yields a member that fails identity checks such as 'value is UNSET'. Code that deep-copies Option or Parameter defaults, or sends them across processes, can then crash or silently take the wrong branch.
findings.suggestion: Restore the three methods, or confirm that the Python versions supported by Click already provide equivalent behaviour for Enum members with object() values and add a test that copies and pickles UNSET and FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE.

findings.title: Concurrent requests to the same host can receive None and bypass robots.txt
findings.description: The removed code wrapped the pending Deferred in a callback that returned the result, so the shared Deferred kept its value for other waiters. Now the shared Deferred is passed directly to maybe_deferred_to_future, which goes through Deferred.asFuture. That adapter adds a callback that sets the future result and returns None. The first waiter therefore resets the shared Deferred's result to None, and every later waiter for the same netloc gets None. process_request_2 treats a None parser as 'allowed', so requests queued behind the first one skip the robots.txt check and are downloaded even when disallowed.
findings.suggestion: Restore the pass-through wrapper: create a new Deferred waiter and add a callback to the shared parser that calls waiter.callback(result) and returns result, then await the waiter. Alternatively, use a Deferred-to-future adapter that does not consume the result.

findings.title: Rejected task is still dispatched after the ETA conversion failure
findings.description: When to_timestamp fails, the code rejects the request with requeue=False, but the early `return` was removed. Execution then continues with eta still None, so the function reaches task_reserved(req), the callbacks and handle(req). A task the broker has just rejected is therefore still queued for execution. This happens on every message whose ETA cannot be converted, such as an out-of-range timestamp.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` immediately after `req.reject(requeue=False)`.

findings.title: Failure result is no longer recorded for the task
findings.description: The removed mark_as_failure call was the only place that stored the conversion error on the result backend. Without it, a task that fails ETA conversion is rejected silently, and clients polling its result never see a FAILURE state with the exception.
findings.suggestion: Restore the mark_as_failure call before the reject, or otherwise record the failure on the result backend.

findings.title: Missing return after reject lets the task run anyway
findings.description: The removed `return` was what stopped execution after an ETA conversion failure. Now, when to_timestamp raises OverflowError or ValueError, the code rejects the request and falls through. `eta` stays None, so the code reaches `task_reserved(req)` and `handle(req)` (or `limit_task` when a rate bucket applies) and dispatches a task that was just rejected. The task may run immediately even though its ETA is invalid, and it may run twice if the broker redelivers the rejected message.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` after `req.reject(requeue=False)` at line 189.

findings.title: Failure is no longer recorded in the result backend
findings.description: The removed `mark_as_failure` call was the only place that stored the conversion error for the task. After this change, a task whose ETA cannot be converted is rejected and only logged. Its result stays PENDING or missing, so clients polling the result never see the failure.
findings.suggestion: Keep the `req.task.backend.mark_as_failure(...)` call before `req.reject(requeue=False)` and the `return` that follows it, unless the failure recording was removed on purpose and this is documented.

findings.title: Rejected request still executes after ETA conversion failure
findings.description: The removed `return` was what stopped processing after `req.reject(requeue=False)`. Now, when `to_timestamp` raises OverflowError or ValueError, `eta` stays None and control falls through. If rate limits are off, the code reaches `task_reserved(req)` and `handle(req)`, so the task runs even though it was rejected. If a rate-limit bucket exists, `limit_task(req, bucket, 1)` queues the rejected request for later execution. A task with a malformed ETA therefore runs anyway, and the rejection has no effect.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` immediately after `req.reject(requeue=False)` at line 189.

findings.title: Failure is no longer recorded in the result backend
findings.description: The removed `mark_as_failure` call was the only place this path wrote the failure to the result backend. With it gone, a task whose ETA cannot be converted is rejected and logged, but its result stays PENDING or unknown, so clients polling the result never see that it failed.
findings.suggestion: Keep the `mark_as_failure` call before `req.reject(requeue=False)` unless its removal is intentional and documented.

findings.title: Cached result list is shared and returned by reference
findings.description: On a cache hit, find returns the same list object stored in the cache. Before this change each call built a fresh list, so callers could mutate the result safely. Now a caller that sorts, appends to, or filters the returned list changes the cached value, and every later call with the same query and tags returns the corrupted result until the TTL expires or a product is added.
findings.suggestion: Return a copy on both hit and miss, for example `return list(entry[1])`, or store and return a tuple.

findings.title: max_entries=0 makes find raise StopIteration
findings.description: With max_entries=0 the check `len(self._cache) >= self._max_entries` is always true, including when the cache is empty. `next(iter(self._cache))` then raises StopIteration on an empty dict, so every find call on a cache miss fails.
findings.suggestion: Reject max_entries < 1 in __init__, or skip caching when max_entries is 0 (for example `if self._max_entries <= 0: return hits`) and evict only when the cache is non-empty.

findings.title: Cached result list is returned by reference and can be mutated by callers
findings.description: find() now stores the list built by _rank in the cache and returns that same list object on every cache hit (here and at line 68 on a miss). Before this change each call returned a fresh list. If a caller sorts, appends to, or otherwise mutates the returned list, the cached entry changes too, so later calls with the same query and tags return the corrupted result until the TTL expires or add() is called.
findings.suggestion: Return a copy, e.g. `return list(entry[1])` on a hit and `return list(hits)` after storing, or store a tuple and convert to a list on return.

findings.title: Cached result list is shared and returned by reference
findings.description: find() stores the list returned by _rank in the cache and returns that same list object on every cache hit. Before this change each call returned a fresh list. If a caller mutates the result (append, sort, remove), the cached entry changes too, so later callers for the same query and tags get corrupted results until the entry expires or a product is added.
findings.suggestion: Return a copy on both paths, for example `return list(entry[1])` on the hit path, or store a tuple and convert to a list on return.

findings.title: max_entries=0 makes find() raise StopIteration
findings.description: The constructor accepts max_entries=0. On a cache miss with an empty cache, len(self._cache) >= 0 is true, so next(iter(self._cache)) runs on an empty dict and raises StopIteration. Any call to find() then fails with a confusing error instead of returning results.
findings.suggestion: Guard the eviction with `if self._max_entries <= 0` (skip caching), or validate max_entries >= 1 in __init__.

findings.title: find() now mutates shared cache state on reads
findings.description: Each find() call pops and reinserts the cache entry, and it may also evict and insert. The class has no locking. Two threads calling find() at the same time can interleave these dict operations, causing a KeyError, a lost entry, or an eviction of the wrong entry. Before this change find() was a pure read.
findings.suggestion: Guard the cache with a lock, or document that SearchService is not thread-safe.

findings.title: Un-awaited coroutine from deliver() is always truthy, so digests are marked delivered and their lines are discarded
findings.description: deliver() is now async, so `deliver(channel, message)` returns a coroutine object without running it. A coroutine object is always truthy, so the branch always runs `del lines[:sent]` and removes queued lines even though the digest was never sent. The coroutine is also never awaited, which raises a RuntimeWarning and means no retries happen. Any recipient's pending notifications are silently lost, and the failed list never reports them.
findings.suggestion: Make flush await the call: `if await deliver(channel, message):`.

findings.title: Missing await on deliver makes every digest look delivered and drops queued lines
findings.description: deliver is now a coroutine function, so `deliver(channel, message)` returns an unawaited coroutine object, which is always truthy. The branch therefore always runs `del lines[:sent]`, and the recipient is removed from the queue even though channel.send was never called. Every pending digest line is silently discarded on each flush, and the 'undelivered ones stay queued' guarantee is broken. The coroutine is also never awaited, which produces a RuntimeWarning.
findings.suggestion: Await the call: `if await deliver(channel, message):`. Also make sure callers of flush await it, since it is now async.

findings.title: Missing await on deliver() makes every digest look delivered
findings.description: deliver() is now a coroutine, but flush() calls it without await. The call returns a coroutine object, which is always truthy, so every recipient is treated as delivered. The digest is never sent, the queued lines are deleted at lines 46-48, and the coroutine is never run (a 'never awaited' warning). Any failed send silently drops user notifications, and the retry logic never runs.
findings.suggestion: Use `if await deliver(channel, message):` so the result of the awaited send is checked.

findings.title: for_account filters on the removed user_id key and always returns nothing
findings.description: records() now passes every line through upgrade_record, which drops the user_id key and moves its value into account_id. The filter record.get("user_id") == account_id therefore never matches, so for_account yields no records for any account, old or new. account_timeline, which is built on it, silently returns an empty list.
findings.suggestion: Filter on the upgraded key: return (record for record in self.records() if record.get("account_id") == account_id).

findings.title: Public functions and store methods renamed without aliases
findings.description: top_users, user_timeline and EventStore.for_user were removed and replaced by top_accounts, account_timeline and for_account, and the Event field user_id became account_id. Existing callers that use the old names or keyword arguments will fail with AttributeError or TypeError after this change.
findings.suggestion: Keep deprecated aliases for the old names that delegate to the new ones, or document the break and update all callers in the same change.

findings.title: for_account filters on the removed user_id key, so it never matches
findings.description: records() now runs every record through upgrade_record, which drops the user_id key and moves its value into account_id. The filter `record.get("user_id") == account_id` therefore never matches any record, old or new. account_timeline depends on for_account, so it always returns an empty list for every account.
findings.suggestion: Filter on the upgraded key: `record.get("account_id") == account_id`.

findings.title: for_account filters on the removed user_id key, so it never matches
findings.description: records() now runs every record through upgrade_record, which drops user_id and writes account_id. The filter record.get("user_id") == account_id therefore never matches stored records, and new records never carry user_id either. for_account returns nothing, so reports.account_timeline always returns an empty list for every account.
findings.suggestion: Filter on the current key: return (record for record in self.records() if record.get("account_id") == account_id).

findings.title: Public report functions and store method renamed without compatibility aliases
findings.description: top_users, user_timeline and EventStore.for_user are removed and replaced by top_accounts, account_timeline and for_account. The Event constructor also drops its user_id keyword in favour of account_id. Existing callers that pass user_id or call the old names will fail with TypeError or AttributeError after this change.
findings.suggestion: Keep deprecated aliases for the old names and accept user_id as a deprecated keyword in Event, or state the break in the change notes.

findings.title: decide() inverts the policy result because check() now returns a list
findings.description: check() changed from returning a bool (True when within policy) to returning a list of violation messages (empty when within policy). decide() still uses it as a boolean: `if check(report, rates):` is truthy when there are violations and falsy when the report is clean. A within-policy report is therefore sent to NEEDS_REVIEW, and an over-limit or missing-receipt report is auto-approved. This bypasses the manager review control for exactly the reports that should be reviewed.
findings.suggestion: Use the list explicitly: `if not check(report, rates):` to approve, or `problems = check(report, rates)` and branch on `if problems:`.

findings.title: decide() inverts the policy result because check() now returns a list
findings.description: check() changed from returning a bool (True when within policy) to returning a list of problems (empty when within policy). decide() still tests the result as a boolean: `if check(report, rates):`. An empty list is falsy, so a compliant report goes to NEEDS_REVIEW, and a report with violations is non-empty, hence truthy, and is auto-APPROVED. Out-of-policy expenses are therefore approved without a manager, and compliant reports are sent to a manager.
findings.suggestion: Test emptiness explicitly: `if not check(report, rates):` (or `problems = check(report, rates)` and branch on `if not problems:`).

findings.title: decide() inverts the policy result because check() now returns a list
findings.description: check() used to return a bool, where True meant within policy. It now returns list[str] of violations, where an empty list means within policy. The truthiness test on line 26 is unchanged, so a report with no violations (empty list, falsy) is sent to NEEDS_REVIEW, and a report with violations (non-empty list, truthy) is auto-APPROVED. Every compliant report now waits for a manager and every non-compliant report is approved without review, which is a financial control failure.
findings.suggestion: Test for emptiness explicitly: `if not check(report, rates):` (or `problems = check(report, rates)` and branch on `if problems:`).

findings.title: create_ticket still passes the old `attempts` keyword, which is now a JSON body field and no longer disables retries
findings.description: The change renames the retry keyword in HelpdeskClient.request from `attempts` to `max_attempts`, but create_ticket still passes `attempts=1`. That value no longer controls retries. It falls into **fields and is sent to the vendor as a body field named "attempts". Because max_attempts keeps its default of 3, a POST /tickets that fails with a transport error or a 5xx is now retried up to three times. If the first request reached the server, each retry can create a duplicate ticket. Before this change, create_ticket was single-attempt.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1` to `max_attempts=1` in create_ticket, matching add_comment.

findings.title: create_ticket still passes the old `attempts` keyword, so POST retries are no longer disabled
findings.description: The rename of the retry parameter from `attempts` to `max_attempts` in client.py means `attempts=1` in create_ticket is no longer consumed by the client. It falls into **fields and is sent as `"attempts": 1` in the JSON body, while the request keeps the default max_attempts=3. A transport error such as a timeout after the server has already created the ticket will cause up to three POSTs, so duplicate tickets are created. The server also receives an unexpected `attempts` field in the body. add_comment was updated to `max_attempts=1`, which shows the intent was to keep this call non-retried.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1` to `max_attempts=1` in the create_ticket call so the client treats it as the retry limit and does not send it in the body.

findings.title: create_ticket still passes attempts=1, which is now a body field, so the POST is retried and can create duplicate tickets
findings.description: The change renames the retry keyword in HelpdeskClient.request from `attempts` to `max_attempts`, but create_ticket still passes `attempts=1`. That value no longer reaches the retry logic. It falls into **fields and is sent as part of the JSON body, and the request uses the default of DEFAULT_ATTEMPTS (3). A POST that times out or has its connection reset with TransportError is therefore retried up to three times. The server may already have created the ticket on the first attempt, so each retry can create a duplicate ticket. The vendor API may also reject or ignore the unknown `attempts` field. Before this change, create_ticket was never retried.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1,` to `max_attempts=1,` in create_ticket, matching add_comment. Also check other callers of client.request that still pass `attempts=`, since they now send it in the body and get the default retries.

findings.title: Sink write failures are recorded as rejected rows and the batch is dropped
findings.description: The try block wraps both parse_row and self._flush. If self._sink.write(pending) raises (for example a database outage, a disk error, or a constraint violation), the exception is caught by the broad except below. The whole pending batch is already detached from `batch` at line 65, so up to batch_size successfully parsed transactions are silently lost. The sink error is then recorded as a single Rejection for the current data row, which is misleading. Loading continues with the next rows, so the report can look mostly clean while data is missing. If the sink keeps failing, each batch is dropped and only the rejection cap eventually raises TooManyRejected, which hides the real cause. Flush calls should sit outside the per-row try, and sink exceptions should propagate.
findings.suggestion: Move the flush out of the try block: keep the try only around parse_row(row), append to batch in the non-raising path, then after the try/except check the batch size and call self._flush outside the exception handler so sink errors propagate unchanged.

findings.title: Malformed rows no longer abort the load; callers must check report.clean
findings.description: The docstring previously stated that the first malformed row aborts the load. Now up to DEFAULT_MAX_REJECTED (1000) malformed rows are skipped silently, and load() returns normally. Existing callers that relied on an exception to detect bad input will now get a successful return with partial data unless they inspect report.rejected. This is a behaviour change to the default path, not just an addition.
findings.suggestion: If this is intentional, document it in the changelog and consider making the default max_rejected=0 so existing callers keep fail-fast behaviour and opt in to skipping.

findings.title: Sink write failures are caught as row rejections, silently dropping batches
findings.description: The try block wraps both parse_row and the mid-stream self._flush call. Any exception from self._sink.write (for example a database outage, a disk error, or a constraint violation) is caught by the broad except Exception and recorded as a Rejection for the current row number. The batch is already detached from `batch` (pending, batch = batch, []), so up to batch_size valid transactions are neither written nor counted in report.loaded, and the loader keeps going. Each later batch can fail the same way until max_rejected is exceeded. The caller gets a report that looks like ordinary data-quality rejections, with the wrong row numbers and no indication that data was lost. A partially completed sink.write is also not surfaced. The final flush at line 72 is outside the try, so the same error there propagates, which makes the behaviour inconsistent.
findings.suggestion: Keep only parse_row inside the try. Move the flush out of it so sink errors propagate, e.g. try: row_t = parse_row(row) except Exception as exc: record rejection; continue; then batch.append(row_t) and flush outside the try block.

findings.title: Sink write failures are recorded as row rejections and the batch is silently dropped
findings.description: The try block wraps both parse_row and the self._flush(pending, report) call. If the sink's write() raises (for example a database outage, disk full, or network error), the exception is caught by `except Exception`, recorded as a Rejection for the current row number with the sink's error text, and the loop continues. Because `pending, batch = batch, []` runs before the flush, the whole batch of up to batch_size rows is discarded without being written or reported as rejected. The load then returns normally, possibly with rejections that blame innocent data rows. Once max_rejected is exceeded, TooManyRejected is raised with a misleading message. Silent data loss is the consequence. Flush failures should propagate, outside the per-row try block.
findings.suggestion: Move the flush out of the per-row try block so only parse_row is guarded, e.g. parse inside try, append to batch, then after the try/except check the batch size and flush outside the exception handler. Let sink errors propagate.

findings.title: Exhausted retries return None instead of raising, so invoices are marked PAID with no charge
findings.description: When the last attempt raises GatewayError, the loop hits `break` and the method falls off the end, returning None despite the `-> Charge` annotation. In settle_invoice, the GatewayError handler never runs. Execution reaches `invoice.status = InvoiceStatus.PAID` (invoices.py line 50), then `charge.id` on None raises AttributeError. The invoice is left persisted as PAID with charge_id unset, and the exception aborts settle_open_invoices, so the rest of the batch is not settled and the counts are lost. Any persistent gateway outage therefore corrupts billing state and crashes the job.
findings.suggestion: After the last failed attempt, re-raise the caught GatewayError (for example, use `raise` inside the except block when attempt == attempts, or keep the last exception and `raise last_exc` after the loop) instead of `break`, so callers see the failure and mark the invoice PAYMENT_FAILED.

findings.title: Retry loop returns None after the final failed attempt instead of raising
findings.description: When the last attempt raises GatewayError, the code logs and executes `break`, so the loop exits and charge() falls off the end and returns None, even though it is annotated to return Charge. The error is swallowed. In settle_invoice, GatewayError is not raised, so the `except` branch is skipped. Execution continues to `invoice.status = PAID` and then `invoice.charge_id = charge.id`, which raises AttributeError on None. That exception escapes settle_open_invoices and aborts the whole batch. The invoice is left marked PAID with no charge_id, and the failed charge is never recorded as PAYMENT_FAILED. Every invoice whose charge fails after all retries triggers this.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise the last GatewayError instead of breaking, for example replace `break` with `raise`, so the caller sees the failure and settle_invoice records PAYMENT_FAILED as intended.

findings.title: Exhausted retries return None instead of raising the gateway error
findings.description: When the final attempt fails, the loop hits `break` and the method falls off the end, so `RetryingGateway.charge` returns None. `settle_invoice` does not catch this. It sets `invoice.status = PAID` at line 50, then reads `charge.id` on None at line 51, which raises AttributeError. That exception escapes `settle_open_invoices` and aborts the whole batch. The invoice is left marked PAID with no charge_id, so the PAYMENT_FAILED path is never reached and the failure is never recorded. Any charge that fails all attempts triggers this.
findings.suggestion: On the last attempt, re-raise the last GatewayError (for example `raise` inside the except block after logging, or `raise exc`) instead of `break`, so the caller's GatewayError handler records PAYMENT_FAILED. Also make sure the function never returns None implicitly.

findings.title: finally clause overwrites the retry schedule, so failed jobs never back off
findings.description: In the except branch, `_run` sets `job.next_run = now + self._retry_delay(job)`. The `finally` block then unconditionally runs `job.next_run = now + job.interval`, which replaces the retry time on every failure. The retry backoff is therefore dead code: a failing job waits a full `interval` before its next attempt, not `retry_delay` doubling up to `interval`. Failures are retried much later than documented, and the Job docstring is wrong about the behaviour.
findings.suggestion: Remove the `finally` and set the schedule explicitly in each branch: `job.next_run = now + self._retry_delay(job)` on failure (already present) and `job.next_run = now + job.interval` in the else branch.

findings.title: Backoff exponent can overflow timedelta and raise out of tick()
findings.description: `_retry_delay` computes `job.retry_delay * 2 ** (job.consecutive_failures - 1)` with no bound. Because `max_failures` is configurable, a job can fail many consecutive times before being disabled. Once the multiplier exceeds timedelta's maximum (roughly 2**50 times a one-minute delay), the multiplication raises OverflowError. That exception is raised from the except block in `_run`, so it escapes `tick()` and stops the scheduler's other jobs for that tick.
findings.suggestion: Cap the exponent before multiplying, for example compare against `job.interval` in integer form or clamp `consecutive_failures - 1` to a small maximum such as 32, then take the min with `job.interval`.

findings.title: Failed jobs are rescheduled at the full interval, so retry backoff never takes effect
findings.description: The new `finally` block unconditionally sets `job.next_run = now + job.interval`, which runs after the except branch has set `job.next_run = now + self._retry_delay(job)`. On every failure the retry time is overwritten, so a failed job waits a full `interval` (for example a day for `daily_at`) before retrying instead of the intended `retry_delay` with exponential backoff. The Job docstring and the `retry_delay` field become misleading, and transient failures recover far more slowly than designed.
findings.suggestion: Remove the `finally` and set `job.next_run = now + job.interval` only in the success branch, or compute the next run once in each branch so the failure path keeps the retry time.

findings.title: Backoff exponent can overflow timedelta and raise from inside the failure handler
findings.description: `2 ** (job.consecutive_failures - 1)` grows without bound, and `max_failures` can be set arbitrarily high. Once `retry_delay * 2**n` exceeds timedelta's maximum (around n=41 with the default one-minute retry_delay), the multiplication raises OverflowError. That exception escapes `_run` from the except branch, so `tick` aborts, the run is not recorded in `history`, and other due jobs in the same tick are skipped.
findings.suggestion: Cap the exponent before multiplying, for example compute the cap as `job.interval` and return it when `consecutive_failures` is large enough that the delay would exceed `job.interval`, or clamp the exponent to a small maximum.

findings.title: finally overwrites the retry delay, so failed jobs never back off
findings.description: In _run, the except branch sets job.next_run = now + self._retry_delay(job) (line 65), but the finally block then unconditionally sets job.next_run = now + job.interval (line 76). finally runs after except, so the retry schedule is always discarded. A failing job is rescheduled after its full interval instead of the intended retry_delay, and the exponential backoff is dead code. Failures that would be retried within a minute are delayed by a whole interval, for example a day for daily_at jobs.
findings.suggestion: Remove the finally block and restore a single assignment after the try/except/else, for example set job.next_run = now + job.interval in the else branch and now + self._retry_delay(job) in the except branch.

findings.title: Backoff exponent can overflow timedelta and raise from inside the failure handler
findings.description: consecutive_failures is unbounded and max_failures can be set arbitrarily high. With 2 ** (consecutive_failures - 1) growing, job.retry_delay * 2**n eventually exceeds timedelta's maximum (around 2**41 minutes-scale multiples), raising OverflowError. That exception is raised inside the except block of _run, so it escapes tick() and prevents the remaining due jobs in that tick from running, and the job is never disabled.
findings.suggestion: Cap the exponent or cap the result before multiplying, for example compare consecutive_failures against a bound derived from interval/retry_delay or compute the delay in seconds with a clamped exponent.

findings.title: Read failures are treated as an empty store, so the next write wipes every session
findings.description: _read_all catches OSError, ValueError and KeyError and returns an empty dict. A transient read error, a truncated or corrupt file, or one malformed record makes every session look absent. save(), delete() and take_by_refresh() then call _write_all with that near-empty dict, which permanently overwrites the file and logs out all users. A single bad record causes the same loss.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a missing file (return empty) from a corrupt or unreadable one (raise StoreError), and never write back after a failed read.

findings.title: Failed revocations after a password change are only logged, so old sessions stay valid
findings.description: sign_out_everywhere swallows StoreError per record and keeps going, and change_password returns the count of successful revocations. If the store fails to delete a session of the user, that session keeps working after the password was changed. The caller only sees a smaller number and a log line, so an attacker holding a stolen session keeps access.
findings.suggestion: Do not swallow the error in change_password. Let StoreError propagate, or retry and fail the whole operation so the caller knows sessions may still be live.

findings.title: Refresh consumes the old session before the new one is saved
findings.description: take_by_refresh removes the old record first. If _issue's save then raises StoreError, the old tokens are already gone and no new session exists, so the user is silently logged out. The client gets an unexpected StoreError instead of a clear result.
findings.suggestion: Save the new session before removing the old one, or make the take and save a single atomic store operation.

findings.title: Every authentication reads and parses the entire session file
findings.description: FileSessionStore.get calls _read_all, which reads and JSON-decodes the whole file. authenticate runs on every request, so the cost grows with the number of live sessions and the file is rewritten on each change.
findings.suggestion: Keep an in-memory index loaded once and updated on writes, or move session storage to a database keyed by access_hash.

findings.title: Unreadable or corrupt session file is treated as empty, so the next write wipes every session
findings.description: _read_all() catches OSError, ValueError and KeyError and returns an empty dict. A transient read failure (permissions, I/O error, a partially written or corrupt file) is therefore indistinguishable from 'no sessions'. The following save() or delete() calls read {}, add or remove one record, and _write_all() overwrites the file with that single record. Every other user's live sessions are silently lost and those users are logged out. The same empty result makes take_by_refresh() return None, so valid refresh tokens are rejected.
findings.suggestion: Only treat a missing file (FileNotFoundError) as an empty store. Let other OSError and ValueError/KeyError propagate, or raise StoreError, so that writes never run on data that was not read successfully.

findings.title: Failed session revocation is logged and skipped, so sessions stay valid after sign-out or password change
findings.description: sign_out_everywhere() catches StoreError from store.delete(), logs a warning, and continues. The session remains usable, and its access token still passes authenticate(). change_password() returns this count as if the sessions had been ended, and callers have no way to know some sessions survived. After a password reset, an attacker holding a stolen session can keep access even though the caller believes all sessions were ended.
findings.suggestion: Do not swallow the error. Let StoreError propagate so the caller fails the request, or collect the failures and raise after attempting the rest, so that change_password can report incomplete revocation.

findings.title: SessionManager constructor and login return type changed in a breaking way
findings.description: The Session dataclass is removed and login() now returns IssuedSession, which has access_token and refresh_token instead of token. The constructor's second positional argument changes from ttl to store, so existing calls such as SessionManager(users, ttl) now pass a timedelta as the store. Callers that read session.token or pass ttl will fail at runtime, and the failure may only appear on the login path.
findings.suggestion: Keep a token attribute or a compatibility alias for callers that still need it, or update every caller in the same change and note the breaking change explicitly.

findings.title: Read failure is treated as an empty store, so the next write erases all sessions
findings.description: _read_all returns {} on any OSError or ValueError. If the session file exists but cannot be read (transient I/O error, permissions, a locked file), save(), delete() or take_by_refresh() call _read_all, get an empty dict, and then _write_all replaces the real file with a file containing only the new record. Every other user's session is lost and those users are logged out. A missing file should be treated as empty, but other read errors should surface as StoreError.
findings.suggestion: Return {} only when the file does not exist (FileNotFoundError). Wrap other OSError and ValueError/KeyError/TypeError from parsing in StoreError so writers abort instead of overwriting the file.

findings.title: Failed revocation during password change leaves sessions alive
findings.description: change_password calls sign_out_everywhere, which logs a warning and continues when store.delete raises StoreError. The caller gets a count that is lower than the number of sessions, but nothing signals failure. A session the attacker holds can survive a password change that was meant to end every session, and the user believes they are signed out everywhere.
findings.suggestion: Do not swallow StoreError in sign_out_everywhere when called from change_password. Propagate the error, or retry and fail the password change, so the caller knows not all sessions were revoked.

findings.title: Constructor signature and session model changed for existing callers
findings.description: SessionManager's ttl parameter is gone and a required store argument was inserted as the second positional parameter. Callers that pass ttl by keyword get a TypeError, and callers that pass ttl positionally now pass it as the store. login() also returns IssuedSession instead of Session, which no longer has a token field, and the default lifetime drops from 12 hours to a 30-minute access token with no refresh call in the old clients, so those clients are logged out after 30 minutes.
findings.suggestion: Keep ttl working as an alias for access_ttl, make store a keyword argument with a default, and document the migration for clients that must call refresh().

findings.title: Whole-file rewrite on every change makes sign-out and purge quadratic
findings.description: FileSessionStore reads and rewrites the full JSON file on each delete. sign_out_everywhere and purge_expired call all() and then delete() for each matching record, so ending N sessions costs N full reads and writes. With a large number of live sessions this becomes slow and blocks other requests on the lock.
findings.suggestion: Add a batch delete method to the store protocol that removes several access hashes in one read and one write, and use it from sign_out_everywhere and purge_expired.

findings.title: Body-only terms get score 0.0, so tagger suggests only title words
findings.description: Terms that do not appear in the title are assigned a score of 0.0 instead of their frequency. suggest_tags in tagger.py keeps only keywords with score >= MIN_SCORE (0.05), so every body-only keyword is filtered out and the only suggestions left are words that also appear in the title. For an article whose title does not repeat its key terms, suggest_tags returns an empty list. The score field also no longer means relative frequency for any caller of extract_keywords.
findings.suggestion: Keep the frequency as the score for every term and add the bonus only when the term is in the title: scores[term] = frequency + (title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0).

findings.title: Body-only terms get score 0.0, so frequency ranking is discarded
findings.description: The new loop sets scores[term] to frequency + title_bonus for title terms but to 0.0 for every other term, so relative frequency is thrown away for body-only words. In tagger.suggest_tags, the MIN_SCORE (0.05) filter then keeps only words that appear in the title, since body-only terms score 0.0. For an article whose title has no candidate words, or an empty title, every score is 0.0 and suggest_tags returns []. Previously frequent body terms were suggested. extract_keywords also changed meaning for callers that do not pass title: all scores become 0.0 and the ranking is alphabetical.
findings.suggestion: Keep the frequency for every term and add the bonus only for title terms: scores[term] = frequency + (title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0), or simply compute frequency and add title_bonus when the term is in title_terms.

findings.title: Body-only terms get score 0.0, so frequency ranking is lost
findings.description: The conditional expression binds as `(frequency + title_bonus) if term in title_terms else 0.0`, so every term that does not appear in the title is scored 0.0 instead of its relative frequency. Before this change those terms were ranked by frequency. Now they all tie at 0.0 and are ordered alphabetically. In tagger.suggest_tags, the MIN_SCORE filter (0.05) then drops every such term, so suggestions are limited to words that appear in the title. Body keywords are effectively never suggested, and the `limit` slots are filled with zero-score terms that are then discarded. The returned Keyword.score values also change meaning for existing callers of extract_keywords.
findings.suggestion: Score every term with its frequency and add the bonus only for title terms: `scores[term] = frequency + title_bonus if term in title_terms else frequency`.

findings.title: Denied token bucket requests refill tokens twice
findings.description: On the denial path, check() stores the refilled token count in bucket.tokens (line 69) but returns before updating bucket.updated_at (line 73 is only reached on success). The next call measures elapsed time from the old timestamp and adds the same refill again. Example with refill_rate 1/s: a bucket is drained at t=0; a cost-5 request at t=1 is denied, leaving tokens=1 with updated_at=0; at t=2 elapsed is 2 so tokens become 3 instead of 2. Repeated denied requests let clients accumulate tokens beyond the intended rate, so the limiter admits more traffic than configured.
findings.suggestion: Set bucket.updated_at = now before the denial return, e.g. move the assignment at line 73 above the `if bucket.tokens < cost` check.

findings.title: Requests whose cost exceeds burst can never succeed
findings.description: If cost is greater than capacity (for example, an expensive endpoint costing 5 with burst or limit set to 3), tokens can never reach cost because they are capped at capacity. Every such request is denied, and retry_after is computed as a finite wait that never leads to success. Clients honoring Retry-After retry forever. The middleware's default burst is `limit`, so this occurs whenever limit is below the expensive cost.
findings.suggestion: Reject or clamp requests where cost > capacity explicitly (for example raise ValueError or return a decision that signals the request can never be admitted), and validate configuration so that burst >= the maximum request cost.

findings.title: Denied requests refill tokens without advancing updated_at, so the same time is credited repeatedly
findings.description: On every call the elapsed time since updated_at is added to tokens (line 69), but updated_at is only set to now on the allowed path (line 73). When a request is denied at line 70-71, the refill is stored in bucket.tokens while updated_at stays at the old value. The next call counts the same interval again. Example: capacity 10, refill_rate 1, tokens 0 at t=0. A check at t=5 is denied with tokens=5. A second check at t=5 computes elapsed=5 again, gives tokens=min(10, 10)=10 and is allowed, though no real time has passed. Repeated rejected requests therefore let a client exceed the configured rate.
findings.suggestion: Set bucket.updated_at = now immediately after the refill on line 69, before the deny check, so the refill is accounted for exactly once.

findings.title: Cost above capacity can never be allowed, so the client is stuck with 429s
findings.description: Tokens are capped at capacity (line 69). If cost is greater than capacity, the condition at line 70 is always true, so the request is always denied. The returned retry_after is computed from a token count that can never reach cost. With the middleware, a bucket built from limit=3 and a default burst of 3 rejects the expensive /v1/search and /v1/export requests (cost 5) permanently, and each reply promises a Retry-After that will not produce success.
findings.suggestion: Reject or clamp costs above capacity explicitly at the start of check (for example raise ValueError at construction when expensive costs are configured, or return a decision that says the request can never be satisfied), and make sure the configured burst is at least the largest request cost.

findings.title: Rejected requests do not advance the bucket timestamp, so refill is credited twice
findings.description: On rejection (lines 70-71), bucket.tokens has already been advanced to the current time by line 69, but bucket.updated_at is not set to now. The early return skips line 73, so the next call computes elapsed from the old timestamp and adds the same refill again. Example with rate 1 token/s and capacity 10: at t=0 the bucket is empty; at t=0.5 a cost-1 request is rejected with tokens=0.5 and updated_at still 0; at t=1 the bucket computes 0.5+1=1.5 tokens when the true value is 1.0. Under sustained over-limit traffic a client gets extra tokens on every rejected call and can exceed the configured rate, potentially up to capacity.
findings.suggestion: Set bucket.updated_at = now before the rejection return, so the refill is credited only once, e.g. move the updated_at assignment above the `if bucket.tokens < cost` check.

findings.title: Previous-month lookup uses the wrong key order, so previous_total is always None
findings.description: UsageKey is (account_id, metric, month), as documented in rollup.py and used in monthly_usage and build_report's own loop unpacking. The lookup builds (account_id, prior, metric), putting the month where the metric belongs and the metric where the month belongs. The lookup therefore never matches, so previous_total is always None and every row shows change 'n/a'. The month-over-month feature, which is the purpose of the report command, does not work.
findings.suggestion: Use the key order used everywhere else: previous = usage.get((account_id, metric, prior)).

findings.title: MONTH_RE with $ accepts a trailing newline, which then matches no rows
findings.description: Python's $ matches before a trailing newline, so a --month value such as '2024-01\n' passes month_arg. The value is then compared against row months with exact equality in build_report, so no rows match and the report silently prints '(no usage)' for a month that has data.
findings.suggestion: Use fullmatch, or \Z in place of $, for example MONTH_RE.fullmatch(value) with the pattern without anchors.

findings.title: Daily grouping can split one day into several totals when timestamps have mixed offsets
findings.description: Events are sorted by absolute timestamp, then grouped by consecutive (account, metric, timestamp.date()) keys. The date is taken from each timestamp's own tzinfo. If the events for one account and metric carry different UTC offsets, the local dates are not monotonic in sort order, so events for the same day can be non-adjacent. The loop then yields that day more than once. monthly_usage counts each yielded group as an active day, so active_days and average_per_active_day are overstated, and peak_day may be computed from a partial total. The docstring promises UTC days, but the code does not convert to UTC before calling .date().
findings.suggestion: Convert each timestamp to UTC before taking .date() (for example event.timestamp.astimezone(timezone.utc).date()), or group with a dict keyed by (account, metric, day) instead of relying on adjacency.

findings.title: MONTH_RE accepts a trailing newline in --month
findings.description: The pattern uses $, which matches before a trailing newline. An argument such as "2024-01\n" passes validation, but build_report compares it to the stored month strings and finds no rows, so the report silently prints "(no usage)" instead of reporting a bad argument.
findings.suggestion: Use \Z instead of $, or compare with fullmatch, e.g. MONTH_RE.fullmatch(value).

findings.title: Month regex accepts a trailing newline, producing a silent empty report
findings.description: Python's `$` matches before a trailing newline, so `MONTH_RE.match` accepts a value such as "2024-01\n". The value then passes validation, `previous_month` parses it because `int()` tolerates whitespace, but `build_report` compares `row_month != month` against keys built by `month_key`, which never contain a newline. The command therefore prints "(no usage)" with exit code 0 instead of rejecting the argument.
findings.suggestion: Use `re.fullmatch` or `\Z` instead of `$`, e.g. `MONTH_RE = re.compile(r"\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])")` used with `fullmatch`.

findings.title: CSV output does not neutralise spreadsheet formula prefixes in account IDs
findings.description: `render_csv` writes `account_id` and `metric` verbatim. If an account ID begins with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, spreadsheet software that opens the exported CSV may evaluate it as a formula, which can exfiltrate data or trigger external requests when a user opens the report.
findings.suggestion: Prefix cells that begin with one of `=+-@` with a single quote or tab in the CSV output path only, and document the behaviour.

findings.title: Mutable default dict shared across calls and mutated by setdefault
findings.description: `metadata` defaults to a single shared `{}`. Line 80 calls `metadata.setdefault("content-type", ...)`, which writes into that shared dict. The first put without metadata stores the content type for its key's extension in the default dict, and later calls that omit metadata reuse it. A .pdf upload can then be stored with a stale or wrong content-type. The same mutation also changes the caller's own dict when one is passed in, which is an unexpected side effect for callers.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None`, build a fresh dict (`meta = dict(metadata or {})`), set the content-type on that copy, and write `meta` to disk without touching the argument.

findings.title: Fixed temp file name for metadata races under concurrent puts to the same key
findings.description: The metadata temp file is always `.<name>.meta.tmp`. Two concurrent puts to the same key both write that file, and the first `os.replace` moves it away. The second `os.replace` then raises FileNotFoundError, so one upload fails. Unique temp names are needed for safe concurrent writes.
findings.suggestion: Create the temp file with `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(dir=path.parent, delete=False)` or `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent)` so each writer gets a unique name, then `os.replace` it.

findings.title: Metadata is replaced before the blob, so a failed blob write leaves them mismatched
findings.description: put() atomically replaces the metadata file first and the blob second. If the blob write fails (disk full, I/O error, interrupted process), the old blob remains with the new metadata, including a possibly different content-type. The docstring says both are written atomically, but the two replaces are not a single transaction.
findings.suggestion: Write the blob first, then the metadata, so a failure before the metadata write leaves the old metadata matching the old blob. Alternatively, store the metadata inside the blob's own record, or roll back the metadata on failure.

findings.title: head() on a directory returns a BlobInfo instead of BlobNotFound
findings.description: head() uses `path.stat()`, which succeeds for directories. Calling head() on a prefix such as "images" when a directory of that name exists returns a BlobInfo with the directory's size and a guessed content type. exists() uses is_file(), so the two methods disagree about whether the key exists.
findings.suggestion: Check `path.is_file()` and raise BlobNotFound otherwise, as exists() does, or use `os.stat` and reject results where `stat.S_ISREG` is false.

findings.title: Mutable default dict leaks content-type between unrelated puts and mutates caller's dict
findings.description: The default argument `metadata: dict[str, str] = {}` is one dict shared by every call that omits `metadata`. Line 80 calls `setdefault` on it, so the first put without metadata stores its guessed content type in the shared default. Later calls that omit metadata keep that stale value because `setdefault` does not overwrite it. For example, put('a.pdf', ...) followed by put('b.png', ...) stores b.png with content-type application/pdf. The same `setdefault` also writes into a caller-supplied dict, so callers see their argument changed. Both are wrong results on a common path.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None`, then build a fresh dict: `meta = dict(metadata or {})` and `meta.setdefault("content-type", guess_content_type(key))`. Serialise `meta` instead of the argument.

findings.title: Metadata is replaced before the blob, so a failed blob write leaves inconsistent state
findings.description: The metadata file is atomically replaced at line 83 before the blob is written at lines 84-86. If `tmp.write_bytes` or `os.replace` fails (for example disk full or permission error), the old blob stays on disk with the new metadata, so head() reports a content type and metadata that do not match the stored bytes. A crash between the two replaces leaves the same mismatch.
findings.suggestion: Write and replace the blob first, then the metadata. If the metadata write fails after the blob has been replaced, remove or roll back the blob, or accept that a stale-metadata window exists and document it.

findings.title: Mutable default metadata dict leaks content-type between calls and mutates caller's dict
findings.description: `metadata: dict[str, str] = {}` is a single dict shared by every call that omits the argument. Line 80 calls `setdefault` on it, so the first put without metadata writes its key's guessed content type into the shared default. Later puts without metadata reuse that stale value, so e.g. put('a.pdf') followed by put('b.png') stores b.png as application/pdf. The same mutation also changes the dict a caller passes in, which the caller does not expect. Fix: use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None`, then build a new dict locally (`meta = dict(metadata or {})`) and call setdefault on that copy.
findings.suggestion: Change the signature to `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None` and do `meta = {**(metadata or {})}; meta.setdefault("content-type", guess_content_type(key))`, then serialise `meta`.

findings.title: Metadata is replaced before the blob, so readers and failures see mismatched state
findings.description: The new metadata file is installed (line 83) before the blob is replaced (line 86). A concurrent head() between the two replaces returns the new content type and metadata with the old blob's size. If the blob write fails (for example disk full in write_bytes), the metadata now describes a blob that was never updated. Writing the blob first would leave at worst stale metadata for the old contents, which is less harmful. A single combined write (such as a manifest) would avoid the window entirely.
findings.suggestion: Write and replace the blob first, then write the metadata, or store the metadata alongside the blob in one atomic unit.

findings.title: Membership test against a list makes unknown-SKU detection quadratic
findings.description: active_skus is a list, so `scan.sku not in active_skus` is a linear scan for every scan. With C active catalog items and S scans, unknown_locations does O(C*S) work, which slows down reconciliation of large stocktakes (tens of thousands of SKUs and scans). Nothing else in reconcile() is this expensive, so this new call becomes the bottleneck.
findings.suggestion: Build a set once: active_skus = {item.sku for item in catalog.active()}. Membership checks then become O(1) and the function runs in O(C+S).

findings.title: Membership test against a list makes unknown-SKU detection quadratic
findings.description: active_skus is a list, so each `scan.sku not in active_skus` is a linear scan over every active SKU. For each scan this costs O(number of active SKUs), so reconcile() is O(scans x active SKUs) overall. With a catalog of tens of thousands of SKUs and a similarly large stocktake, this becomes tens of billions of comparisons and reconcile() will take minutes or hours where it previously ran in linear time. The new unknown_locations pass is what introduces this cost.
findings.suggestion: Build a set once: active_skus = {item.sku for item in catalog.active()}. Membership tests then become O(1) and the function is linear in the number of scans and SKUs.

findings.title: Linear list membership test on every scan makes unknown-SKU detection quadratic
findings.description: active_skus is a list, so `scan.sku not in active_skus` scans the whole list for each scan. A stocktake with N scans and M active catalog items costs O(N*M) in unknown_locations, which runs on every reconcile call. For large catalogs and scan volumes this becomes noticeably slow, and the cost is new with this change.
findings.suggestion: Build a set once: active_skus = {item.sku for item in catalog.active()}. Membership checks then become O(1) and the function becomes O(N+M).

findings.title: Holidays are re-fetched on every business-day check
findings.description: The per-year holiday cache was removed. is_business_day calls holidays(day.year) on every call, and holidays() now calls the source each time. With JsonHolidaySource, each call re-reads and re-parses the whole JSON file. add_business_days and business_days_between call is_business_day once per calendar day, so a single due-date computation can trigger many file reads and parses. Computing overdue tickets for a batch becomes very slow.
findings.suggestion: Restore caching per (region, year) inside BusinessCalendar, or cache the parsed data in JsonHolidaySource so the file is read once.

findings.title: overdue() return type changed from tuples to OverdueTicket objects
findings.description: overdue previously returned list[tuple[Ticket, date]]. It now returns list[OverdueTicket]. Existing callers that unpack pairs, such as `for ticket, due in policy.overdue(...)`, or index with pair[1], will raise TypeError or read the wrong values. Callers are not updated in this change.
findings.suggestion: Keep returning (ticket, due) tuples from overdue() and add a separate method for OverdueTicket records, or update every caller in the same change.

findings.title: One ticket with an unconfigured region aborts the whole overdue report
findings.description: due_date calls for_region, which raises KeyError for any region not configured in CalendarSet. overdue() iterates all tickets without catching this, so a single ticket with a stray or misspelled region code makes the entire overdue computation fail. overdue_by_region only groups by configured codes, so it does not help here.
findings.suggestion: Validate ticket regions at ingestion, or have overdue() catch the error per ticket, report those tickets separately, and keep processing the rest.

findings.title: Holiday lookup is no longer cached, so each business-day check re-reads the source
findings.description: The previous BusinessCalendar cached holidays per year. The new holidays() calls self._source.holidays() on every call, and is_business_day() calls it for every day it checks. With JsonHolidaySource that means reading and parsing the whole holiday JSON file for each day visited. add_business_days and business_days_between loop over many days, so a single due_date computation can re-read the file dozens of times, and overdue() over many tickets multiplies that further.
findings.suggestion: Restore per-year caching in BusinessCalendar (e.g. a dict keyed by year), or cache the parsed file in JsonHolidaySource, so the source is read once per region and year.

findings.title: start_day now takes a Ticket instead of a datetime, breaking existing callers
findings.description: start_day previously accepted a datetime (opened_at). It now accepts a Ticket and reads ticket.opened_at and ticket.region. Any caller that still passes a datetime will fail with AttributeError, and SlaPolicy's constructor also changed from (calendar, cutoff_hour) to (calendars), so existing construction sites break too.
findings.suggestion: If the signature change is intended, document it and update all call sites. Otherwise keep start_day(opened_at: datetime) and add a separate method or an optional region parameter.

findings.title: Holiday lookup is no longer cached, so every day check re-reads the holiday source
findings.description: The per-year cache was removed. is_business_day calls holidays(day.year) for every day it tests, and holidays() now calls self._source.holidays() each time. With JsonHolidaySource that re-reads and re-parses the whole JSON file per day, so add_business_days and business_days_between cost one file read and parse per calendar day. Long horizons or many tickets in overdue() make this very slow.
findings.suggestion: Cache the frozenset per (region, year) inside BusinessCalendar, or load the holiday data once in the source and reuse it.

findings.title: Holiday file format changed, so existing data files are rejected
findings.description: JsonHolidaySource now expects a region-keyed file ({"PT": {"2026": [...]}}). Files in the previous flat format ({"2026": [...]}) have no region keys, so every region lookup raises UnknownRegion. Deployments that still use the old file fail on their first business-day calculation.
findings.suggestion: Migrate the existing holiday files to the new shape before deploying, or accept the legacy flat format as a fallback for a single region.

findings.title: overdue() now returns OverdueTicket objects instead of (ticket, due) tuples
findings.description: The return type changed from list[tuple[Ticket, date]] to list[OverdueTicket]. Callers that unpack pairs, index with [0] or [1], or compare against tuples will break at runtime.
findings.suggestion: Keep the tuple return for overdue(), and add a separate method for the richer OverdueTicket result.
