findings.title: Ticket gained a required region field, breaking existing constructors
findings.description: The new region field has no default, so every existing Ticket(id, opened_at, priority) call raises TypeError. Tickets without a region also cannot be placed in any calendar.
findings.suggestion: Give region a default that maps to a known region, or migrate all call sites in the same change.

findings.title: One ticket with an unconfigured region aborts the whole overdue report
findings.description: due_date calls CalendarSet.for_region, which raises KeyError for an unknown region. Because overdue() iterates every ticket without catching it, one bad ticket in a batch makes the whole report fail, and overdue_by_region fails with it.
findings.suggestion: Catch the KeyError per ticket and report those tickets separately, or validate regions before building the report.

findings.title: Non-refusal send errors discard the partial campaign report
findings.description: send_campaign only catches RecipientRefused. Any other exception from mailer.send, such as a dropped SMTP connection or a timeout, propagates out of the loop. The CampaignReport built so far, which records who was already sent to, is lost. A caller retrying the campaign cannot tell which subscribers already received the message, so they may be emailed twice or skipped.
findings.suggestion: Catch the broader error at the send call, record it in the report (for example in a failed map), and decide explicitly whether to continue or stop. Alternatively, attach the partial report to the re-raised exception.

findings.title: Non-refusal send errors abort the whole campaign and discard the report
findings.description: send_campaign only catches RecipientRefused. Any other exception from mailer.send (for example a transient SMTP connection error or timeout) propagates out of the loop. The caller then gets no CampaignReport, so it cannot tell which subscribers already received the campaign. A retry would resend to those subscribers, and the remaining subscribers are silently skipped.
findings.suggestion: Catch the transient mailer error types per recipient and record them in the report (or re-raise with the partial report attached), so that a single failure does not discard the results of earlier sends.

findings.title: Calibration is loaded once per reading instead of once per sensor
findings.description: The previous summarize() loaded one calibration per distinct sensor_id. The new loop calls calibrated(), which calls source.load(reading.sensor_id), for every reading. With a SQL-backed CalibrationSource this issues one query per reading, so a batch of N readings costs N database round trips where it previously cost one per sensor. On large batches this slows summarization sharply and adds load on the database.
findings.suggestion: Load calibrations once per distinct sensor before the loop, for example calibrations = {s: source.load(s) for s in {r.sensor_id for r in batch}}, then apply them per reading. This requires materialising the iterable, as the old code did.

findings.title: New positional field inserted in ZoneSummary shifts existing positional arguments
findings.description: `rejected` is inserted between `count` and `mean`, and `mean`, `low` and `high` become Optional. Any caller that constructs ZoneSummary positionally, or that reads a field by index, will now bind values to the wrong fields or fail. Callers that use keyword arguments are unaffected.
findings.suggestion: Add `rejected` as the last field with a default of 0, or keep the original field order and append the new field at the end.

findings.title: Calibration is loaded once per reading instead of once per sensor
findings.description: The previous summarize() loaded one calibration per distinct sensor_id. The new loop calls calibrated(), which calls source.load() for every reading. With a SqlCalibrationSource this issues one database query per reading, so a batch of N readings costs N queries where it previously cost one per sensor. Large batches will be slow and put avoidable load on the database.
findings.suggestion: Restore the per-sensor cache: load calibrations for the distinct sensor_ids in the batch (materialise the iterable first), then apply each reading using the cached calibration, or memoise source.load within summarize().

findings.title: Calibration is now loaded once per reading instead of once per sensor
findings.description: The previous summarize() materialised the batch and loaded each sensor's calibration once. The new loop calls calibrated(), which calls source.load() for every reading. With a SQL-backed CalibrationSource this issues one query per reading, so a large batch causes N+1 queries and noticeably slower runs for the same result.
findings.suggestion: Cache calibrations per sensor_id within summarize(), for example with a dict filled lazily from source.load(), and apply the cached calibration in the loop. Keep the streaming loop if that matters, since the cache only holds one Calibration per sensor.

findings.title: Every bid check re-reads and re-parses the full day's impression log
findings.description: can_bid now calls spend(), which calls log.for_day(), which opens the day's JSONL file and json-parses every record. eligible() calls can_bid() once per campaign, so one bid request reads the same file once per campaign (and each read parses all campaigns' records to keep only one). Before this change, spend was kept in memory and updated on record(). With many campaigns and a busy day this makes every bid request cost O(campaigns x day's impressions) of disk I/O and JSON parsing, on the hot bidding path, which can exceed bid timeouts under load.
findings.suggestion: Compute spend for all campaigns in one pass per request (or cache per-day totals and update them in record()/refund()), and invalidate or adjust the cache when mark_invalid is called, instead of re-reading the log for each campaign.

findings.title: Every bid re-reads and parses the whole day's impression log per campaign
findings.description: can_bid now calls self.spend(), which calls log.for_day(), which opens and json-parses the entire day's JSONL file on every call. eligible() calls can_bid for every campaign, so each bid request reads the log once per campaign. Log size grows with traffic, so per-request cost grows with the day's volume, and at bid-request rates this adds heavy disk I/O and CPU on the hot path. The previous version kept running totals in memory.
findings.suggestion: Cache per-campaign, per-day hourly totals and update them in record() and refund(), or memoise spend() for the current day and invalidate it on writes, so bidding does not re-read the file for each request.

findings.title: Every bid request re-reads and re-parses the full day's impression log for each campaign
findings.description: can_bid now calls self.spend, which calls JsonlImpressionLog.for_day, which opens the day's JSONL file, json-parses every line, and builds the invalid-id set. eligible() calls can_bid once per campaign, so each bid request reads the same day file once per campaign. With many campaigns and a day's log that grows to hundreds of thousands of lines, this turns each bid into O(campaigns x log size) disk I/O and JSON parsing on the hot serving path, and latency rises as the day progresses. The previous implementation kept per-day spend in memory and updated it on record().
findings.suggestion: Compute spend for all campaigns in one pass per request or per day, or keep an in-memory per-day aggregate that is updated on record() and refund() and rebuilt from the log on startup.

findings.title: Empty locale tag now raises ValueError from build_bundle
findings.description: fallback_chain calls parents(locale), which calls normalise(). normalise raises ValueError for an empty or whitespace-only tag. Before this change, build_bundle accepted any string and simply returned the key-as-message bundle. Any caller that passes an empty locale, such as a missing or blank Accept-Language value or an unset user preference, now gets an exception on the request path where it previously rendered a page.
findings.suggestion: Catch ValueError around fallback_chain and fall back to default_locale only, or validate the locale at the boundary and substitute DEFAULT_LOCALE for empty input.

findings.title: Bundle.locale is now the normalised chain head, not the requested locale
findings.description: The Bundle is built with locale=chain[0], so a request for 'pt_br' now yields bundle.locale 'pt-BR' instead of 'pt_br'. That value feeds to_json() and missing_report() keys, which changes output that callers may compare or key on. The catalog is also now queried with the normalised tag, so a catalog stored under raw tags would miss lookups.
findings.suggestion: If the rename is not intended, keep the requested locale in Bundle.locale and use the normalised value only for lookups. If it is intended, document the change and check consumers of to_json() and missing_report().

findings.title: `missing` now means absent in every locale, not just the requested one
findings.description: Before this change, `Bundle.missing` listed keys with no translation in the requested locale. Now a key found only in a parent or the default locale is recorded in `sources` and not in `missing`. `missing_report` is built from `missing`, so for a pt-BR request that falls back to English, translators no longer see those keys in the report. Callers that relied on `missing` to flag untranslated keys will silently stop receiving them.
findings.suggestion: Keep `missing` as keys not found in the requested locale, for example by appending to it when the matched candidate is not chain[0], and let `fallback_keys` cover the fallback case. Alternatively, rename the field and update `missing_report` to match the intended meaning.

findings.title: Empty or blank locale now raises ValueError instead of rendering
findings.description: `fallback_chain` calls `normalise`, which raises `ValueError` for an empty or whitespace-only tag. Before this change, `build_bundle` accepted any locale string. If a request arrives without a locale, for example an empty Accept-Language value, this call now raises on the page path rather than falling back to the default locale.
findings.suggestion: Catch the empty-tag case in `build_bundle` and substitute `default_locale`, or validate the locale at the request boundary so the error is handled there.

findings.title: Per-key catalog lookups replace the batched get_many call
findings.description: The old code made one catalog.get_many(locale, wanted) call. The new loop calls catalog.exists and then catalog.get for every key and every candidate in the fallback chain, so a page with N keys and a chain of length C makes up to about 2*N*C catalog calls. If the catalog is backed by a database or remote store, this becomes an N+1 query pattern, and it is slower on every page render even when the key is found in the requested locale.
findings.suggestion: Fetch each candidate locale once with a batched call (for example get_many per chain entry on the still-unresolved keys), then assign each key from the first locale that has it, so the number of catalog round trips is bounded by the chain length rather than the key count.

findings.title: Bundle.locale now holds the normalised fallback head, not the requested locale
findings.description: Previously Bundle.locale was the locale the caller passed in. It is now chain[0], the normalised tag, so a request for 'pt_br' yields locale 'pt-BR' and to_json emits that value. Callers that compare bundle.locale with the requested string, or that key caches or templates on it, will see different values. Note also that a locale with no subtags that is empty now raises ValueError from normalise instead of returning an empty bundle.
findings.suggestion: If callers depend on the requested tag, keep Bundle.locale as the input value and store the resolved head separately, or document the change and check the callers.

findings.title: Any reader can delete a journal entry they do not own
findings.description: delete_entry checks only _require_reader, which passes for anyone in entry.readers. store.remove then permanently deletes the entry for everyone. A user who was merely shared a read-only entry can destroy the owner's data. Every other mutating handler (edit, share, unshare) uses _require_owner, so this is an authorisation gap.
findings.suggestion: Call _require_owner(entry, user) instead of _require_reader(entry, user) in delete_entry. Readers who want to stop seeing the entry should use leave_entry.

findings.title: Any reader can delete a journal entry
findings.description: delete_entry checks only _require_reader, which passes for any user in entry.readers. A shared reader can therefore call delete_entry and permanently remove an entry they do not own, along with its data for the owner and all other readers. Only the owner should be able to delete it, as the error message in leave_entry and the owner-only edit/share/unshare handlers imply.
findings.suggestion: Replace _require_reader(entry, user) with _require_owner(entry, user) in delete_entry.

findings.title: Any reader can delete the owner's journal entry
findings.description: delete_entry guards with _require_reader, which admits any user in entry.readers. A user who was shared an entry can therefore call delete_entry and permanently remove it through store.remove, destroying the owner's data for all readers. Only the owner should be able to delete. The owner-only helper _require_owner exists and is used by edit_entry, share_entry and unshare_entry, so this is an authorisation inconsistency.
findings.suggestion: Replace _require_reader(entry, user) with _require_owner(entry, user) in delete_entry, so that only the owner can delete. Readers who want to stop seeing the entry should use leave_entry.

findings.title: accept() does not check link expiry
findings.description: accept() only rejects revoked links and links that have used up max_uses. It never checks expires_at or is_active(now), so an expired invite link still adds new members to the workspace with the link's role. The now argument is passed in but never used for the validity check.
findings.suggestion: Reject the link when not link.is_active(now), or when now >= link.expires_at, before calling directory.add.

findings.title: Invite codes generated with non-cryptographic random
findings.description: _new_code() uses random.choices, which is the Mersenne Twister PRNG and is predictable once enough output is observed. Invite codes are bearer tokens that grant workspace membership, so an attacker who can infer the generator state can guess valid codes and join workspaces.
findings.suggestion: Generate codes with secrets.choice (or secrets.token_urlsafe) so that they come from a cryptographically secure source.

findings.title: Expired invite links can still be accepted
findings.description: accept() only rejects links that are revoked or used up. It never checks link.expires_at, so a link past its expiry still adds new members with the link's role. is_active() checks expiry, but accept() does not call it. Anyone holding an old code can join the workspace after the owner expected the link to be dead.
findings.suggestion: Reject expired links in accept(), for example by checking `now < link.expires_at` or by calling `link.is_active(now)` and raising InviteNotUsable when it is false.

findings.title: Invite codes generated with non-cryptographic random
findings.description: _new_code() uses random.choices, which is a Mersenne Twister PRNG and is predictable once its state is inferred from observed outputs. Invite codes act as bearer credentials that grant workspace membership, so an attacker who can observe enough codes could predict unissued ones and join workspaces they were not invited to.
findings.suggestion: Generate codes with the secrets module, for example `secrets.choice(CODE_ALPHABET)` in a loop of CODE_LENGTH, or `secrets.token_urlsafe`, and keep the uniqueness check.

findings.title: accept() does not check link expiry, so expired invite links remain usable
findings.description: accept() rejects only revoked links and links that have reached max_uses. It never checks expires_at, so a link past its expiry is still accepted and grants membership. is_active() includes the expiry check, but accept() does not call it. Any holder of an expired code can join the workspace for as long as the link stays in the dictionary, which is until purge() removes it after 90 days past creation.
findings.suggestion: Reject the link when now >= link.expires_at, for example by checking `not link.is_active(now)` before adding the member, and raise InviteNotUsable.

findings.title: Invite codes are generated with the non-cryptographic random module
findings.description: _new_code() uses random.choices, which is a Mersenne Twister PRNG. Its output can be predicted from observed values, and it is not suitable for bearer credentials. Invite codes grant workspace membership, so an attacker who observes a few codes could predict others and join workspaces through links they were never given.
findings.suggestion: Generate codes with the secrets module, for example "".join(secrets.choice(CODE_ALPHABET) for _ in range(CODE_LENGTH)).

findings.title: Any logged-in user can issue complimentary tickets
findings.description: comp_tickets only calls require_login, so any authenticated attendee can call tickets.comp and receive free tickets for any event and any holder_id. Comp issuance is a staff or admin function, as the attendee list endpoint's role check shows, so this bypasses the intended access control and lets ordinary users take unpaid capacity.
findings.suggestion: Call require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) in comp_tickets, as attendee_list does, before issuing comps.

findings.title: Any logged-in user can issue free complimentary tickets
findings.description: comp_tickets only calls require_login, so any authenticated attendee can call the tickets.comp route. It creates zero-price tickets for any holder_id, up to 50 per request with no limit on repeated requests. The sibling admin route cancel_event and the staff route attendee_list both enforce a role, so this endpoint is an authorization bypass that lets ordinary users mint free tickets and consume event capacity.
findings.suggestion: Replace require_login with require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) (or the intended comp role), keeping the user object for issued_by.

findings.title: Any logged-in user can issue complimentary tickets
findings.description: comp_tickets only calls require_login, so any authenticated attendee can call tickets.comp with any event_id and holder_id. Each call creates free tickets (price 0) that count against event capacity, so an ordinary user can issue comps to arbitrary holders and exhaust capacity or give away paid inventory. The sibling attendee_list and cancel_event handlers gate on roles, and comps should be restricted the same way.
findings.suggestion: Replace the require_login call with require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) (and keep the user id for issued_by), so that only staff or admins can issue complimentary tickets.

findings.title: move_card does not check edit rights on the source board
findings.description: move_card loads the card by id and checks only that the actor is an editor of the target board. It never checks the card's current board. An actor who is an editor on board B can move a card that lives on a private board A where they are not a member. The card then leaves board A, its title and description become visible on board B, and the card is detached from A's column. Non-members of A should get NotFound for that card, as they do elsewhere.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) on the card's current board before moving it, in addition to the target-board check.

findings.title: move_card never checks editor access on the source board
findings.description: move_card loads the card with self._store.card(card_id) and only checks editor rights on the target board. A user who is an editor of any board (or has no access to the card's current board at all) can pass the id of a card on a board they cannot edit, and it is detached from its source board and moved into their own board. This breaks the privacy rule stated in _require_role (non-members should get NotFound) and lets users remove or alter cards on other users' boards. The check should be applied to card.board_id before the move.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) right after loading the card, in addition to the check on to_board_id.

findings.title: move_card checks only the target board, so a card can be pulled from a board the actor cannot edit
findings.description: move_card fetches the card by id and then checks editor role only on to_board_id. It never checks the card's current board (card.board_id). An editor of board B can therefore move any card from board A, where they are a non-member or viewer, into board B by passing its id. Card ids are sequential and enumerable. edit_card and archive_card both check editor rights on card.board_id, so this path bypasses the access rule the rest of the service enforces. The result is unauthorised relocation of cards between boards, and the card's data becomes visible to the attacker's board.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) on the source board as well as on the target board before moving the card. Consider raising NotFound for non-members on the source board, to match _require_role.

findings.title: Partner-domain check matches any host that merely ends with the domain string
findings.description: `host.endswith(domain)` has no label boundary, so with partner domain `shop.example` an attacker-controlled origin such as `https://evilshop.example` or `https://attackershop.example` passes `is_allowed`. `response_headers` and `preflight_headers` then echo that origin in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so a malicious site can make credentialed cross-origin requests to `/v1/balance` and `/v1/redeem` using a logged-in member's session cookie and read the responses.
findings.suggestion: Match on a label boundary: accept when `host == domain or host.endswith('.' + domain)`, and add a test with a lookalike host such as `evilshop.example`.

findings.title: Partner domain match has no label boundary, so look-alike domains get credentialed CORS
findings.description: is_allowed uses host.endswith(domain) with a bare suffix. A partner domain of shop.example also matches an attacker-registered host such as noshop.example or evilshop.example, and example.com matches badexample.com. For those origins response_headers and preflight_headers return Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. A malicious page on such a domain can then make credentialed requests to /v1/balance and /v1/redeem with the member's session cookie, reading balances and spending points.
findings.suggestion: Require a dot boundary or exact match: return host == domain or host.endswith('.' + domain), and apply the same check in the settings validation path if needed.

findings.title: Partner domain match accepts unrelated domains that merely end with the same string
findings.description: is_allowed uses host.endswith(domain) without requiring a dot boundary. With partner domain shop.example, an origin such as https://evilshop.example or https://attackershop.example passes the check and receives Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. A malicious site on such a domain can then make credentialed cross-origin requests to /v1/balance and /v1/redeem using the member's session cookie, reading balances and spending points.
findings.suggestion: Match the domain exactly or as a dot-separated suffix, for example: host == domain or host.endswith('.' + domain).

findings.title: Connection never released when reserve() raises an InventoryError
findings.description: The `self._pool.release(conn)` call on line 96 sits after the try/except, not in a finally block. The except branch re-raises, so every InventoryError (InsufficientStock, UnknownSku, DuplicateReservation) exits the function before release runs. Each rejected reservation, which is a common business outcome when stock is short, leaks a pooled connection. Under load the pool is exhausted and later callers block or fail. Non-InventoryError exceptions (for example a database error) also skip both rollback and release.
findings.suggestion: Move the release into a finally block, as cancel() and level() already do: wrap the try/except in try/finally and call self._pool.release(conn) in the finally clause, keeping conn.rollback() in the except path.

findings.title: Connection is never released when reserve() raises an InventoryError
findings.description: The self._pool.release(conn) call sits after the try/except. The except block re-raises, so whenever UnknownSku, InsufficientStock or DuplicateReservation is raised, control leaves reserve() before line 96 runs and the connection is never returned to the pool. Each rejected reservation (for example, an order that cannot be fully stocked) leaks one connection, and once the pool is exhausted, later callers block or fail. Non-InventoryError exceptions, such as database errors, also skip both rollback and release.
findings.suggestion: Move the release into a finally block, as cancel() and level() already do: wrap the try/except in an outer try whose finally calls self._pool.release(conn).

findings.title: Connection is never released when reserve() rejects an order
findings.description: In reserve(), the except InventoryError branch calls conn.rollback() and then re-raises. The self._pool.release(conn) call sits after the try/except, so it is skipped on every InventoryError path (DuplicateReservation, UnknownSku, InsufficientStock). Each rejected order leaks a pooled connection. Once the pool is exhausted, later acquire() calls block or fail, so the whole inventory service stops responding.
findings.suggestion: Move the release into a finally block that wraps the whole try, for example: try: ... except InventoryError: conn.rollback(); raise finally: self._pool.release(conn).

findings.title: Non-inventory exceptions skip rollback, leaving an open transaction on the connection
findings.description: reserve() rolls back only on InventoryError. If conn.put or conn.commit raises a database error or any other exception mid-loop (for example a connection drop or a serialization failure), the partial reserved-count updates are not rolled back. Since the connection is also not released on that path, the open transaction may later be committed by another caller or stay half-applied.
findings.suggestion: Catch BaseException (or use try/except/else) so that rollback runs for every failure, then re-raise. Combine this with releasing the connection in a finally block.

findings.title: cancel() does not roll back when a mid-loop failure occurs
findings.description: cancel() decrements reserved counts per SKU and then deletes the reservation. If conn.get, conn.put or conn.delete raises partway through, there is no rollback. The finally block releases the connection with uncommitted writes still pending. Depending on the pool, those writes can leak into a later transaction, leaving stock reserved counts out of step with the reservation record.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the body in try/except that calls conn.rollback() and re-raises on failure, and commit only on success.

findings.title: Missing stock row in cancel() raises an unhelpful TypeError
findings.description: If a reservation references a SKU whose stock row is absent, conn.get returns None and row['reserved'] raises TypeError. The caller sees a generic TypeError with no SKU context, and the whole cancel is aborted without a clear error.
findings.suggestion: Check for None and raise UnknownSku(sku) with a clear message, or document why this state cannot occur.

findings.title: Duplicate upload leaves its temp file in incoming/ forever
findings.description: put_stream writes every upload to incoming/upload-<uuid>. When the digest already exists (target.exists() is true), the function returns early without unlinking that temp file, so the data stays on disk. Only the success path (os.replace) and the exception path remove it. Every duplicate upload, which is common for content-addressed storage, leaks a full copy of the blob, so disk usage grows without bound.
findings.suggestion: Unlink the incoming file before returning on the duplicate path, for example incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True) before the return, or restructure so cleanup runs in a finally block whenever the file was not moved into place.

findings.title: Uploaded temp file is leaked when the blob already exists
findings.description: put_stream writes the full upload to a file under incoming/ and only moves it into place with os.replace on the create path. When target.exists() is true, the function returns early at line 66 without removing the incoming file, so every duplicate upload leaves a full-size copy behind in the incoming directory. Because the content is already stored, these orphaned files accumulate without bound and consume disk space, and the pre-change code did not have this problem.
findings.suggestion: Remove the temporary file before returning on the dedup path, for example by calling incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True) before the early return, or restructure so the cleanup runs in a finally block whenever the file was not moved.

findings.title: Duplicate uploads leave their temporary file in incoming/
findings.description: put_stream writes every upload to a unique file under incoming/ and only renames it when the blob is new. When target.exists() is true (the common deduplication case), the function returns without removing incoming, so each duplicate upload leaves a full copy of the blob on disk. Disk usage grows with every repeated upload, and the incoming directory is never cleaned up. The same leak happens if mkdir or os.replace fails after the file is written, because those calls are outside the try/except.
findings.suggestion: On the already-exists path, call incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True) before returning. Also move the parent mkdir and os.replace inside a try that unlinks incoming on failure.

findings.title: Eviction loop counts countries instead of entries, so the cache is effectively unbounded
findings.description: _store compares len(self._keys_by_country), the number of distinct countries, against max_entries. The cache holds up to max_entries rates, so the check should use len(self._entries). With a handful of countries the loop never runs, and every distinct (country, postal_code) pair is kept indefinitely. Expired entries are only replaced when the same key is looked up again, so memory grows with the number of distinct postal codes requested, and the cache_size setting has no effect. Eviction also only starts once the country count exceeds the limit, which is not the documented behaviour.
findings.suggestion: Change the loop condition to `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:`. Entries and _keys_by_country stay consistent because _evict_oldest removes the key from both.

findings.title: Eviction loop counts countries instead of cached entries, so the cache never bounds its size
findings.description: _store compares len(self._keys_by_country), the number of distinct countries, against max_entries. The cache holds up to max_entries rates per country, so a single country can grow without limit (for example, many distinct postal codes for one country). Eviction only starts once more than max_entries countries are cached. Under sustained lookups for one country, memory grows unbounded and the max_entries limit does nothing. The previous lru_cache(maxsize=4096) bounded this.
findings.suggestion: Compare the total entry count: `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:` and keep the per-country index in sync in _evict_oldest, which already handles that.

findings.title: Cache size bound counts countries instead of entries, so the cache grows without limit
findings.description: _store compares len(self._keys_by_country), the number of distinct countries, against max_entries. The cache holds up to one entry per (country, postal_code) pair, so with a handful of countries the cache never evicts, however many postal codes are looked up. Memory grows with every distinct postal code requested, and the cache_size limit and the evictions metric do not behave as documented. Eviction should depend on the number of cached entries.
findings.suggestion: Change the loop condition to `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:`.

findings.title: Retry returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of an Event
findings.description: In enrich_one, the retry branch is `return enrich(event, geo)` without await. enrich is async, so the function returns a coroutine object. _flush then passes that coroutine to sink as if it were an Event, so to_json fails or writes garbage. Any lookup that times out once breaks the run.
findings.suggestion: Change the line to `return await enrich(event, geo)`.

findings.title: Counting lines consumes the input iterator, so nothing is processed
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` exhausts `lines`. When lines is a file object or other one-shot iterator (as cli.py passes), the later `for line in lines` loop sees no items. The run reads zero lines, writes nothing, and reports zero counts, so the output file is empty.
findings.suggestion: Materialise the input first, for example `lines = list(lines)`, which costs memory on large exports. Or drop the up-front total and report progress against an unknown total.

findings.title: Counting lines consumes the input iterable before processing
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` exhausts `lines` before the main loop runs. The CLI passes a file object, which is a one-shot iterator, so the `for line in lines` loop sees nothing. The run reports zero read, zero written, and produces an empty destination file with no error.
findings.suggestion: Materialise the input first (for example `lines = list(lines)`), or drop the total count and report progress without a denominator, or pass a re-iterable source.

findings.title: Retry returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of an Event
findings.description: In the `except LookupTimeout` branch, `return enrich(event, geo)` returns the coroutine object rather than awaiting it. `_flush` then passes that coroutine to `sink`, where `to_json` fails or writes garbage. Any lookup that times out once crashes the run or corrupts the output.
findings.suggestion: Change the line to `return await enrich(event, geo)`.

findings.title: Counting lines consumes the input iterator, so nothing is enriched or written
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` exhausts `lines` before the main loop runs. The CLI passes an open file object, which is a one-shot iterator, so the later `for line in lines:` loop sees no lines. The run reports read=0 and writes no events, and the destination file is silently left empty. This affects every run, not only edge cases.
findings.suggestion: Materialise the input once (for example `lines = list(lines)`) before counting, or obtain the total from a separate pass over the file, or drop the total and report progress without it.

findings.title: Retry returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of an Event
findings.description: `enrich` is now async, but the retry branch returns `enrich(event, geo)` without `await`. `enrich_one` therefore returns a coroutine object rather than an Event. When that object reaches `sink`, `to_json` fails on it, or it is written as garbage, and Python emits a 'coroutine was never awaited' warning. Any lookup that times out once crashes or corrupts output on the retry path.
findings.suggestion: Change the line to `return await enrich(event, geo)`.
